newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - NZ faces slim IPO pickings in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - NZ faces slim IPO pickings in 1997.

text.p: New Zealand faces the prospect of a handful of initial public offerings (IPOs) this year but fresh opportunities are otherwise expected to be limited, market analysts say.

Pepsico Inc was first off the block last week when it revealed its plan to sell its New Zealand operations through an IPO, which will see ownership of its 122 New Zealand restaurants pass to Restaurant Brands NZ Ltd.
The float of 85 million shares between NZ$1.80-2.20 each will value the company at NZ$187 million (US$272 million) if the institutional tender prices them at the top of the range.
This will put the company among New Zealand's top 40 by market capitalisation and will make it the largest public offer since Tranz Rail last June.
Among the issues pending is property investment company CBD New Zealand Ltd, which is seeking to raise between NZ$19.5 million and $29.5 million.
The developers of Auckland's Britomart complex, Pacific Capital Assets, are planning a NZ$50 million public issue as part of a possible share market listing.
Healthcare property investor Calan Group plans to raise around NZ$50 million through a share market float later this year.
Infratil is planning an international version of what it does domestically -- invest in infrastructure and utilities.
And New Zealand investors are showing great interest in the Australasian float of Colonial Mutual, the offer having closed last week substantially over-subscribed.
BROKERS SEE NO RUSH TO LIST
While there are other IPO possibilities yet to be detailed, brokers do not expect a great rush to the listing board here.
"It's relatively lean pickings when you compare it with what's been happening offshore in terms of new IPOs," Robert Bode, head of research at Merrill Lynch, told Reuters.
"There has not been a lot of supply pressure and we've come through a period where there have been many stocks effectively removed from the market," he said.
Skellerup Ltd disappeared from the board last year after a management buyout, and Whitcoulls Group Ltd met the same fate after being taken over by U.S. Office Products.
Wang unit Wang New Zealand and U-Bix Business Machines are expected to delist soon after the virtual completion of their takeovers, also by U.S. Office.
Likewise, Underground Fashions is soon expected to be completely engulfed by Kymbyr Investments.
BOURSE WEIGHTINGS DO NOT REFLECT BROAD ECONOMY
Brokers said the New Zealand share market presents a distorted picture of the economy, Telecom NZ having a massive 25.17 percent weighting on the NZSE-40 Capital Index.
Collectively, forest sector stocks Fletcher Paper, Fletcher Forests and Carter Holt Harvey have a 19 percent weighting.
Brierley Investments, with the bulk of its assets overseas, has a 7.15 percent weighting and Lion Nathan, with more than 70 percent of its assets in Australia, accounts for a four percent weighting.
All up, the top 10 companies represent 65 percent of total market capitalisation.
"Those large companies are influenced by commodity markets and overseas equity markets," Bode said.
"It's not a good reflection of the New Zealand economy, so there is good demand for New Zealand pure-play exposures," he said.
Among the few new listings over the last 12-18 months, Lyttleton Port, Tranz Rail and Mainfreight have performed strongly relative to the market.
But the leadup to last October's general election, plus tight monetary conditions over the first quarter, may have quelled any new listing ambitions.
EASIER CONDITIONS MAY BRIGHTEN IPO OUTLOOK
A market-led easing in monetary conditions may have brightened the IPO outlook somewhat, but lower rates would also ease the cost of funding and lessen the need for capital.
On top of that, New Zealand's long-running privatisation phase appeared to be nearing completion.
New issuers also face the barrier of size.
"You need to be floating companies of reasonable size to get the liquidity and widespread institutional/retail support, domestically and internationally," Bode said.
Looking ahead, the areas of the economy likely to need fresh capital are the infrastructure sectors, where water, sewerage and electricity generation offer possibilities.
Cavill White principal Don Turkington said there was strong demand for new issues, as evidenced by the enthusiasm for the Colonial float, both here and in Australia.

"If there are any half-way reasonable floats that come to the market they will be well received, despite the poor performance of the market. People are really interested in new possibilities," he said. "But the thing is they have to be substantial businesses," he added.

Talk at the start of the year, when the market was strong, of an abundance of new issues may have proved premature, Turkington said. "Now it's not so good, but most of these things are long term," he said. ($ = 0.686 New Zealand Dollars)
